issues.name: The Economy & Jobs
issues.blurb: Recovery from the pandemic recession, jobs, and the stock market.

issues.name: COVID-19 Response
issues.blurb: Masks, lockdowns, vaccines, and the federal pandemic response.

issues.name: Healthcare
issues.blurb: The ACA, pre-existing conditions, and the cost of care.

issues.name: Immigration
issues.blurb: The border, DACA, and the family-separation legacy.

issues.name: Race & Policing
issues.blurb: Policing reform and racial justice after the summer of protest.

issues.name: Climate & Energy
issues.blurb: Wildfires, the Green New Deal, and fracking.

issues.name: Taxes & Spending
issues.blurb: Who pays, the 2017 cuts, and stimulus checks.

issues.name: Law & Order
issues.blurb: Crime, unrest in the cities, and 'defund the police'.

issues.name: Abortion & the Courts
issues.blurb: The Supreme Court vacancy and the future of Roe.

issues.name: Trade & Manufacturing
issues.blurb: China, tariffs, and the industrial Midwest.

pandemicIssue.name: Pandemic Response
pandemicIssue.blurb: A deadly epidemic, closed schools and businesses, and who handles it better.

dem.name: Kamala Harris
dem.blurb: Coalition builder. Shores up Black and suburban-women turnout and sharpens the debate stage.

dem.name: Elizabeth Warren
dem.blurb: Progressive firebrand. Electrifies college whites and the youth vote and floods the small-dollar pipeline.

dem.name: Amy Klobuchar
dem.blurb: Midwestern pragmatist. Rebuilds the blue wall with non-college whites and seniors.

dem.name: Gretchen Whitmer
dem.blurb: Battleground governor. A tireless surrogate who locks in suburban Michigan and the upper Midwest.

dem.name: Val Demings
dem.blurb: Former police chief. Blunts the law-and-order attack and energizes Black and senior voters.

rep.name: Mike Pence
rep.blurb: Evangelical anchor. Guarantees the base, holds non-college whites and seniors, steadies the debate.

rep.name: Nikki Haley
rep.blurb: Suburban bridge. Wins back suburban women and college whites the top of the ticket bleeds.

rep.name: Tim Scott
rep.blurb: Outreach closer. A magnetic fundraiser who softens the margins with Black and suburban voters.

rep.name: Tom Cotton
rep.blurb: Hardliner. Maximizes non-college turnout and runs hot on law and order.

rep.name: Kristi Noem
rep.blurb: Heartland energy. A relentless campaigner who runs up the score in rural America.

scenarios.label: 1932 · Roosevelt v. Hoover
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1932. A quarter of the workforce is unemployed, the banks are failing, and veterans were driven from Washington by the army. The governor of New York promises a new deal. The President says recovery is under way.

runningMates.name: John Nance Garner
runningMates.blurb: The Speaker from Texas: his delegates went to Roosevelt on the fourth ballot, and he took second place.

runningMates.name: Al Smith
runningMates.blurb: The Happy Warrior: the 1928 nominee, beloved by Catholic and immigrant voters in the cities.

runningMates.name: Newton Baker
runningMates.blurb: Wilson's War Secretary: a respected Ohio lawyer and the stop-Roosevelt compromise candidate.

runningMates.name: Albert Ritchie
runningMates.blurb: Maryland's governor: a states' rights wet who campaigns against Prohibition.

runningMates.name: Charles Curtis
runningMates.blurb: The sitting Vice President from Kansas: a farm-state veteran of the Senate.

runningMates.name: Charles Dawes
runningMates.blurb: Coolidge's Vice President and a Nobel laureate: floated as a replacement for Curtis, but he declined.

runningMates.name: Hanford MacNider
runningMates.blurb: The Iowa war hero and former Legion commander: a pitch to veterans.

runningMates.name: Ogden Mills
runningMates.blurb: Hoover's Treasury Secretary: the administration's sharpest defender on the stump.

scenarios.evNote: 1930-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Alaska and Hawaii were territories and DC had no electors.

issues.name: The Depression
issues.blurb: Bank failures, farm foreclosures, and one worker in four without a job.

issues.name: Relief for the Jobless
issues.blurb: Whether Washington should feed and employ the unemployed or leave relief to states and charity.

issues.name: Balancing the Budget
issues.blurb: Hoover's 1932 tax increase and Roosevelt's pledge to cut federal spending.

issues.name: Prohibition & Order
issues.blurb: Repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment, bootleg crime, and the army clearing the Bonus marchers.

issues.name: The Tariff
issues.blurb: Smoot-Hawley's high duties, collapsing farm exports, and foreign retaliation.

scenarios.label: 1936 · Roosevelt v. Landon
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1936. The New Deal on trial: Social Security, the WPA and a recovery still under way. The Liberty League's money is against the President, and so is the Literary Digest poll. The voters are another matter.

runningMates.name: John Nance Garner
runningMates.blurb: Cactus Jack: the Texas Vice President who keeps the conservative South on the ticket.

runningMates.name: Alben Barkley
runningMates.blurb: Kentucky's senator: a loyal New Deal floor man and a fine stump speaker.

runningMates.name: Joseph Robinson
runningMates.blurb: The Senate majority leader from Arkansas: the man who passed the New Deal.

runningMates.name: Herbert Lehman
runningMates.blurb: New York's governor: a 'little New Deal' at home and strength in the big Northern cities.

runningMates.name: Frank Knox
runningMates.blurb: The Chicago Daily News publisher: a Rough Rider and a hard-hitting critic of the New Deal.

runningMates.name: Arthur Vandenberg
runningMates.blurb: Michigan's senator: turned the slot down, and would have helped in the auto states.

runningMates.name: William Borah
runningMates.blurb: The Lion of Idaho: a progressive maverick with a following of his own in the West.

runningMates.name: Styles Bridges
runningMates.blurb: New Hampshire's young governor: a fresh face for a party that lost a generation in 1932.

scenarios.evNote: 1930-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Alaska and Hawaii were territories and DC had no electors. Lemke's Union Party vote is left out of the two-party map.

issues.name: Recovery
issues.blurb: Four years of the New Deal: millions back at work, but one worker in six still idle.

issues.name: Social Security
issues.blurb: The new old-age pensions, and the payroll deduction Republicans called a cut in the pay envelope.

issues.name: Spending & Deficits
issues.blurb: Relief spending, the 1935 wealth tax, and a budget that has not balanced since 1930.

issues.name: Farms & Trade
issues.blurb: The farm program the Supreme Court struck down, soil conservation payments, and Hull's trade deals.

issues.name: Anti-Lynching Bill
issues.blurb: The stalled federal anti-lynching bill, as Black voters move toward Roosevelt.

issues.name: The Constitution
issues.blurb: The Liberty League's charge that the New Deal tramples the Constitution and the Court.

issues.name: The Dust Bowl
issues.blurb: Drought, dust storms, and soil conservation across the Great Plains.

scenarios.label: 1940 · Roosevelt v. Willkie
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1940. France has fallen, Britain fights alone, and Roosevelt breaks the two-term tradition. A businessman who has never held office won the Republican nomination from nowhere. Keep the country out of the war, or ready for it.

runningMates.name: Henry Wallace
runningMates.blurb: The Agriculture Secretary: Roosevelt's own pick for a farm-belt New Dealer, forced on a reluctant convention.

runningMates.name: William Bankhead
runningMates.blurb: The Speaker from Alabama: the Southern conservatives' candidate and a comfort to the South.

runningMates.name: Paul McNutt
runningMates.blurb: Indiana's former governor: handsome, ambitious, and strong in the Midwest.

runningMates.name: James Byrnes
runningMates.blurb: South Carolina's senator: a deal-maker who keeps the Southern conservatives in line.

runningMates.name: Charles McNary
runningMates.blurb: The Senate minority leader from Oregon: a farm and public-power man who backed parts of the New Deal.

runningMates.name: Robert Taft
runningMates.blurb: Ohio's senator: Mr. Republican, the isolationist Old Guard's own man.

runningMates.name: Thomas E. Dewey
runningMates.blurb: The racket-busting New York prosecutor: the primary front-runner Willkie overtook.

runningMates.name: Arthur Vandenberg
runningMates.blurb: Michigan's senator: still an isolationist in 1940, and a voice for the industrial Midwest.

scenarios.evNote: 1930-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Alaska and Hawaii were territories and DC had no electors.

issues.name: The War in Europe
issues.blurb: Aid to Britain, the destroyers-for-bases deal, and the first peacetime draft.

issues.name: Jobs & Recovery
issues.blurb: Unemployment near 15 percent as defense orders begin to revive industry.

issues.name: Business & Spending
issues.blurb: Willkie's case that New Deal spending and regulation hold business back.

issues.name: New Deal Programs
issues.blurb: Social Security, relief and labor law, which Willkie pledged to keep in some form.

issues.name: Farm & Trade Policy
issues.blurb: Farm price supports and the reciprocal trade agreements with Latin America.

issues.name: Segregated Forces
issues.blurb: Black leaders press Roosevelt to open the expanding army and defense plants to Black workers.

issues.name: Aliens & Refugees
issues.blurb: The Alien Registration Act and fear of a fifth column as refugees flee Europe.

scenarios.label: 1944 · Roosevelt v. Dewey
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1944. Allied armies are closing on Germany and Japan, and the President wants a fourth term. A young New York governor says the home front needs new hands. The President's health is the question nobody can ask out loud.

runningMates.name: Harry S. Truman
runningMates.blurb: The Missouri senator: his war-contracts committee made his name, and the party bosses trust him.

runningMates.name: Henry Wallace
runningMates.blurb: The sitting Vice President: labor and the left want him kept, and the Southern bosses want him gone.

runningMates.name: James Byrnes
runningMates.blurb: The 'assistant president' for the home front: a South Carolinian labor and Black voters distrust.

runningMates.name: William O. Douglas
runningMates.blurb: The young justice: a Westerner with New Deal credentials and no enemies in the convention hall.

runningMates.name: John Bricker
runningMates.blurb: Ohio's governor: an Old Guard conservative who balances a New York internationalist.

runningMates.name: Earl Warren
runningMates.blurb: California's new governor: declined the slot, and would have brought the West Coast.

runningMates.name: Leverett Saltonstall
runningMates.blurb: Massachusetts' governor: a Yankee moderate for the industrial Northeast.

runningMates.name: Harold Stassen
runningMates.blurb: Minnesota's former governor, now serving in the Navy: a war record and the young internationalist wing.

scenarios.evNote: 1940-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Alaska and Hawaii were territories and DC had no electors.

issues.name: Winning the War
issues.blurb: D-Day, the island fighting in the Pacific, and who should see the war through.

issues.name: Postwar Jobs
issues.blurb: Fear that unemployment will return to Depression levels when war production ends.

issues.name: Wartime Taxes
issues.blurb: Payroll withholding, record tax rates, and Congress overriding Roosevelt's tax veto.

issues.name: Veterans & Security
issues.blurb: The GI Bill for returning servicemen and the future of Social Security.

issues.name: The Poll Tax
issues.blurb: Southern poll taxes, the Court's ban on the white primary, and fair employment in war plants.

issues.name: Postwar Trade
issues.blurb: Bretton Woods and whether America stays in world trade after the war.

scenarios.label: 1948 · Truman v. Dewey
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1948. Every poll says Dewey. The Democrats have split three ways: Thurmond's Dixiecrats in the Deep South and Wallace's Progressives on the left. Truman has a train and a Congress to run against.

runningMates.name: Alben Barkley
runningMates.blurb: The Veep-to-be: a Kentucky Senate leader whose keynote speech brought the convention to its feet.

runningMates.name: William O. Douglas
runningMates.blurb: The New Deal justice: Truman's first choice, a liberal who could hold the Wallace-curious left.

runningMates.name: Sam Rayburn
runningMates.blurb: Mr. Sam: the Texas House leader, a reassurance to Southern Democrats tempted by Thurmond.

runningMates.name: Hubert Humphrey
runningMates.blurb: The Minneapolis mayor whose civil rights speech split the convention: all in on the North.

runningMates.name: Earl Warren
runningMates.blurb: California's governor: a popular moderate who balances a New York ticket with the West.

runningMates.name: Charles Halleck
runningMates.blurb: The House majority leader: Indiana's party man, and a link to the Congress Truman is running against.

runningMates.name: Harold Stassen
runningMates.blurb: Dewey's primary rival: the young Midwestern internationalist he beat in Oregon.

runningMates.name: Arthur Vandenberg
runningMates.blurb: The Senate's foreign-policy elder: the face of the bipartisan Cold War consensus.

scenarios.evNote: 1940-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Thurmond carried Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina (38 votes) and won one Tennessee elector; there is no third slot, so as with Wallace in 1968 his vote in those four states is counted against the Democrat and they open in the Republican column. Truman was not on the Alabama ballot. Wallace's Progressive vote is left out of the two-party map.

issues.name: Prices & Housing
issues.blurb: Postwar inflation, meat and housing shortages, and the 'do-nothing' 80th Congress.

issues.name: Civil Rights
issues.blurb: Truman's order to desegregate the armed forces and the Dixiecrat walkout.

issues.name: Communism & the Cold War
issues.blurb: The Berlin Airlift, the Marshall Plan, and Wallace's call for peace with Moscow.

issues.name: Taxes
issues.blurb: The Republican tax cut Congress passed over Truman's veto in April.

issues.name: Labor & the Fair Deal
issues.blurb: Repealing the Taft-Hartley curbs on unions, national health insurance, and public housing.

issues.name: Farm Prices
issues.blurb: Falling crop prices and the Republican Congress's limits on federal grain storage.

issues.name: Displaced Persons
issues.blurb: The 1948 law admitting European refugees, which Truman signed while calling it discriminatory.

scenarios.label: 1952 · Stevenson v. Eisenhower
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1952. Twenty years of Democratic presidents, a stalemate in Korea, and the most famous general in the world on the Republican ticket. An Illinois governor has to talk sense to a country that wants a change.

runningMates.name: John Sparkman
runningMates.blurb: Alabama's New Deal senator: a Southern moderate chosen to hold the South after the 1948 walkout.

runningMates.name: Estes Kefauver
runningMates.blurb: The crime-hearings star: won the primaries and the television audience, and has the party bosses against him.

runningMates.name: Richard Russell
runningMates.blurb: Georgia's Senate leader: the segregationist South's own candidate, and a hard sell in the North.

runningMates.name: Mike Monroney
runningMates.blurb: Oklahoma's reform senator: a border-state voice for clean government.

runningMates.name: Richard Nixon
runningMates.blurb: The young California senator: the Hiss case made his name, and he gives the general an attack dog and the West.

runningMates.name: Earl Warren
runningMates.blurb: California's popular governor: a progressive Republican who wins Democratic votes at home.

runningMates.name: Harold Stassen
runningMates.blurb: Minnesota's former boy governor: an internationalist who moved his delegates to Eisenhower.

runningMates.name: Walter Judd
runningMates.blurb: The missionary doctor from Minnesota: a powerful orator and an anti-communist voice on Asia.

scenarios.evNote: 1950-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Alaska and Hawaii were territories and DC had no electors.

issues.name: Korea & Communism
issues.blurb: The stalemated war in Korea, McCarthy's charges, and the fear of Soviet spies.

issues.name: Prices & Controls
issues.blurb: Wartime price controls, the steel strike, and Truman's seizure of the steel mills.

issues.name: The Mess in Washington
issues.blurb: Bribery in the tax bureau, high wartime taxes, and Eisenhower's promise to clean house.

issues.name: Civil Rights
issues.blurb: Fair employment laws and the Senate filibuster, with Stevenson courting the South.

issues.name: The Fair Deal
issues.blurb: Social Security, public housing, and Truman's stalled national health insurance plan.

issues.name: Farm Supports
issues.blurb: Price supports for farmers and Eisenhower's pledge to keep full parity.

issues.name: The McCarran Act
issues.blurb: The immigration law passed over Truman's veto, keeping national-origins quotas.

scenarios.label: 1956 · Stevenson v. Eisenhower
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1956. Peace, prosperity and a popular general with a heart attack behind him. Stevenson tries again with a New America program, and the farm belt is restless. Two crises abroad are a few weeks away.

runningMates.name: Estes Kefauver
runningMates.blurb: The coonskin-cap crusader: a Tennessee senator who won the open convention vote and works the small towns.

runningMates.name: John F. Kennedy
runningMates.blurb: The young senator from Massachusetts: nearly won the open floor vote, and brings Catholic voters in the Northern cities.

runningMates.name: Albert Gore Sr.
runningMates.blurb: Tennessee's other senator: a New Deal Southerner who refused to sign the Southern Manifesto.

runningMates.name: Hubert Humphrey
runningMates.blurb: Minnesota's liberal: labor, farm and civil rights credentials for the upper Midwest.

runningMates.name: Richard Nixon
runningMates.blurb: The sitting Vice President: a tireless partisan campaigner who does the attacking so the President does not have to.

runningMates.name: Christian Herter
runningMates.blurb: The dump-Nixon alternative: a Massachusetts governor and diplomat favored by the party's moderates.

runningMates.name: William Knowland
runningMates.blurb: The Senate Republican leader from California: an Old Guard conservative with a hard line on China.

runningMates.name: Charles Halleck
runningMates.blurb: The Indiana congressman and former House majority leader: a farm-belt organizer for the restless Midwest.

scenarios.evNote: 1950-census apportionment: 48 states and 531 electoral votes, 266 to win. Alaska and Hawaii were territories and DC had no electors. One Alabama elector voted for Walter B. Jones; the model gives Stevenson all eleven.

issues.name: Prosperity
issues.blurb: Record employment and output, against Democratic charges of tight money and shrinking farm income.

issues.name: The H-Bomb & Suez
issues.blurb: Stevenson's call to stop H-bomb tests, the Suez crisis, and the Soviet crushing of Hungary.

issues.name: Integration
issues.blurb: Brown v. Board, the Montgomery bus boycott, and the Southern Manifesto.

issues.name: Taxes & the Budget
issues.blurb: A balanced budget, and Democratic charges that Republican tax cuts favored the rich.

issues.name: Social Security
issues.blurb: Disability insurance added to Social Security that summer, and aid for schools.

issues.name: Farm Prices
issues.blurb: Falling farm income and Secretary Benson's flexible price supports.

scenarios.label: 1960 · Kennedy v. Nixon
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1960. Television changes everything, the Cold War is at the podium, and a hundred thousand votes decide it all. Win the debate, and win the century's closest race.

runningMates.name: Lyndon Johnson
runningMates.blurb: The Master of the Senate: a Texas titan who holds the Solid South on the ticket.

runningMates.name: Stuart Symington
runningMates.blurb: Missouri's air-power senator: a safe border-state hand with defense credibility.

runningMates.name: Adlai Stevenson
runningMates.blurb: The two-time nominee: an eloquent liberal beloved by the party's intellectuals.

runningMates.name: Hubert Humphrey
runningMates.blurb: The primary rival: labor's champion and a bridge to the liberal North.

runningMates.name: Henry Cabot Lodge
runningMates.blurb: The UN ambassador: Boston Brahmin polish and Cold War gravitas for the suburbs.

runningMates.name: Nelson Rockefeller
runningMates.blurb: New York's new governor: an Eastern moderate who firms up the big industrial states.

runningMates.name: Barry Goldwater
runningMates.blurb: Arizona's conscience of a conservative: red meat for the Sun Belt right.

runningMates.name: Thruston Morton
runningMates.blurb: Kentucky's party chairman: a border-South organizer to guard the upper South.

scenarios.evNote: 1950-census apportionment: 537 electoral votes, with none for DC until 1964. Maine and Nebraska voted statewide; their district units stand in, with the at-large unit holding the rest of each state's votes. The 15 Byrd electors have no third slot and are folded into the two-party map.

issues.name: Recession & Growth
issues.blurb: The 1960 recession and Kennedy's pledge to get the country moving again.

issues.name: The Cold War
issues.blurb: The missile gap, Castro's Cuba, the U-2 incident, and Quemoy and Matsu.

issues.name: Spending & the Budget
issues.blurb: Nixon's warning that Kennedy's programs would cost billions or mean higher taxes.

issues.name: Medical Care for the Aged
issues.blurb: Health insurance for retirees through Social Security, blocked in Congress that summer.

issues.name: Civil Rights
issues.blurb: Sit-ins across the South and Kennedy's call to Coretta Scott King.

issues.name: Farm Surpluses
issues.blurb: Grain surpluses, falling farm income, and the cost of price supports.

issues.name: Kennedy's Religion
issues.blurb: Whether a Catholic president would answer to Rome, and his Houston pledge on church and state.

scenarios.label: 1964 · Johnson v. Goldwater
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1964. A martyred president's heir, a landslide already forming, and a nuclear ad that only aired once. Ride the tide, or find out how deep the Sun Belt runs.

runningMates.name: Hubert Humphrey
runningMates.blurb: The Happy Warrior: the liberal conscience of the party and its bridge to labor and civil rights.

runningMates.name: Eugene McCarthy
runningMates.blurb: Minnesota's poet-senator: a cerebral liberal with college-town appeal.

runningMates.name: Robert Kennedy
runningMates.blurb: The Attorney General: the martyred president's brother and keeper of the flame.

runningMates.name: Sargent Shriver
runningMates.blurb: The Peace Corps founder: idealism and a Kennedy connection for a grieving country.

runningMates.name: William Miller
runningMates.blurb: The New York congressman: a partisan brawler chosen because, in Goldwater's words, he drives Johnson nuts.

runningMates.name: Nelson Rockefeller
runningMates.blurb: The vanquished moderate: the Eastern establishment Goldwater ran against, and the suburbs' last hope.

runningMates.name: George Romney
runningMates.blurb: Michigan's moderate governor: a reluctant reach for the industrial Midwest.

runningMates.name: Richard Nixon
runningMates.blurb: The loyal soldier: the 1960 nominee, campaigning hard to keep the party whole.

issues.name: Prosperity & Poverty
issues.blurb: The boom after the Kennedy tax cut and Johnson's War on Poverty.

issues.name: The Civil Rights Act
issues.blurb: The 1964 law Goldwater voted against, and the backlash across the Deep South.

issues.name: Nuclear War & Vietnam
issues.blurb: Goldwater's talk of nuclear weapons, the Gulf of Tonkin, and the Daisy ad.

issues.name: Big Government
issues.blurb: Goldwater's case against federal power, spending, and the progressive income tax.

issues.name: Social Security & Medicare
issues.blurb: Medicare for the elderly, and Goldwater's idea of making Social Security voluntary.

issues.name: Farm Supports
issues.blurb: Goldwater's plan to phase out farm price supports, a hard sell on the Plains.

issues.name: School Prayer & Morality
issues.blurb: The Court's school prayer rulings and Goldwater's warnings of moral decline.

scenarios.label: 1968 · Humphrey v. Nixon
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1968. A party split three ways, a burning summer behind it, and a law-and-order pitch aimed at the middle. Wallace holds the Deep South, and the road to 270 runs through the wreckage.

runningMates.name: Edmund Muskie
runningMates.blurb: The calm from Maine: a steady, plain-spoken senator who reassures a fractured party.

runningMates.name: Ted Kennedy
runningMates.blurb: The surviving brother: the one name that could heal the wound of a terrible summer.

runningMates.name: Fred Harris
runningMates.blurb: Oklahoma's populist: a young prairie liberal who reaches the New Deal heartland.

runningMates.name: Sargent Shriver
runningMates.blurb: The War on Poverty's architect: a Kennedy in-law with idealist appeal.

runningMates.name: Spiro Agnew
runningMates.blurb: The law-and-order governor: a blunt Marylander pitched at the backlash vote.

runningMates.name: Nelson Rockefeller
runningMates.blurb: The Eastern moderate: the dream ticket for the suburbs and the big industrial states.

runningMates.name: Ronald Reagan
runningMates.blurb: The conservative insurgent: California charisma and the movement's rising hope.

runningMates.name: George Romney
runningMates.blurb: Michigan's earnest governor: a manufacturing moderate for the industrial Midwest.

scenarios.evNote: 1960-census apportionment. Wallace's five-state sweep is folded into the two-party map, so the model returns a Nixon win without a third slot.

issues.name: Vietnam & Law and Order
issues.blurb: The war and the Paris talks, riots after King's murder, and Nixon's promise of order.

issues.name: Civil Rights & the Cities
issues.blurb: Open housing, the Kerner report on the riots, and Wallace's segregationist run.

issues.name: Prices & Jobs
issues.blurb: Low unemployment but rising prices as war spending heats the economy.

issues.name: The War Surtax
issues.blurb: The 10 percent income surtax Johnson signed in June to pay for the war.

issues.name: The Great Society
issues.blurb: Medicare, Medicaid, and the antipoverty programs Nixon promised to trim.

issues.name: Permissiveness
issues.blurb: Campus revolt, drugs, and the permissive society Nixon and Wallace campaigned against.

scenarios.label: 1972 · McGovern v. Nixon
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1972. A prairie liberal against a landslide in the making. The war, the counterculture, and a break-in nobody is talking about yet. Fight the tide, or ride it to 520.

runningMates.name: Sargent Shriver
runningMates.blurb: The Peace Corps founder: a late-substitute Kennedy in-law with a sunny disposition.

runningMates.name: Thomas Eagleton
runningMates.blurb: The original pick: a Missouri Catholic for the border states, before the medical story broke.

runningMates.name: Ted Kennedy
runningMates.blurb: The last brother: the ticket that never was, and the only name that could unite the party.

runningMates.name: Hubert Humphrey
runningMates.blurb: The Happy Warrior: a primary rival whose old coalition McGovern desperately needs.

runningMates.name: Spiro Agnew
runningMates.blurb: The incumbent attack dog: red meat for the base and the nattering nabobs of negativism.

runningMates.name: John Connally
runningMates.blurb: The Democrats for Nixon chairman: a Texas power broker who raids the other coalition.

runningMates.name: Nelson Rockefeller
runningMates.blurb: The Eastern establishment: a moderate reach for the suburbs and the big states.

runningMates.name: Ronald Reagan
runningMates.blurb: California's governor: the future of the movement, waiting in the wings.

issues.name: The War & Watergate
issues.blurb: Ending the Vietnam War, amnesty for draft evaders, and the Watergate break-in.

issues.name: Wage & Price Controls
issues.blurb: Nixon's wage and price controls, inflation, and unemployment near 6 percent.

issues.name: Busing
issues.blurb: Court-ordered busing to integrate schools, which Nixon asked Congress to halt.

issues.name: Taxes & Welfare
issues.blurb: McGovern's $1,000 grant for every American and his plan to tax large inheritances.

issues.name: Social Security
issues.blurb: The 20 percent Social Security increase Congress passed that summer.

issues.name: Acid, Amnesty, Abortion
issues.blurb: The social issues label pinned on McGovern, months before Roe v. Wade.

issues.name: The Soviet Grain Deal
issues.blurb: The huge 1972 wheat sale to Moscow and what it did to farm and bread prices.

issues.name: Pollution
issues.blurb: The Clean Water Act, passed over Nixon's veto in October, and the new EPA.

scenarios.label: 1976 · Carter v. Ford
scenarios.tagline: Fall, 1976. A pardon still hangs in the air, the country wants a clean start, and a peanut farmer runs against Washington itself. Hold the Solid South, or watch the map slip away.

runningMates.name: Walter Mondale
runningMates.blurb: Labor's friend from Minnesota: a liberal workhorse who firms up the union North.

runningMates.name: Frank Church
runningMates.blurb: Idaho's liberal lion: Western reach and Senate stature on foreign policy.

runningMates.name: John Glenn
runningMates.blurb: The astronaut-senator: Ohio, and a name every household already trusts.

runningMates.name: Henry 'Scoop' Jackson
runningMates.blurb: Cold War Democrat: defense credibility and blue-collar Washington muscle.

runningMates.name: Bob Dole
runningMates.blurb: The Kansas hatchet man: a sharp-tongued attack dog who locks down the farm belt.

runningMates.name: Ronald Reagan
runningMates.blurb: The primary rival: unite the party and electrify the conservative base.

runningMates.name: Howard Baker
runningMates.blurb: Tennessee's Great Conciliator: a Watergate star with border-South reach.

runningMates.name: John Connally
runningMates.blurb: The Texas heavyweight: a Democrat-turned-Republican who plays for the Sun Belt.

issues.name: Jobs & Inflation
